summary: This informational memo describes a way to protect a router's control plane, the part that runs routing protocols and management, from unwanted or malicious traffic. The operator first identifies all legitimate control-plane traffic, then installs a filter in the forwarding path that blocks everything else from reaching the router's brain. It also discusses how to find and maintain that list of legitimate flows.

plainLanguage.summary: A router must process some packets for routing and management, but too many unwanted packets can overload it. This RFC describes filtering those packets before they reach the router's control plane.

questions: how to protect router control plane
how to stop attack traffic reaching a router cpu
how can a router protect its control plane
subtitle: A method for filtering unwanted traffic before it reaches a router's control plane

tldr.problem: A router's control plane handles routing and management traffic using resources that can be more vulnerable to overload than the forwarding hardware.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC identifies traffic the router must process, then applies filters and rate limits in the forwarding plane to traffic destined for the router itself.
tldr.outcome: The document provides a method and example configurations, not a universal filter. Operators must identify legitimate traffic for their own network.

today: RFC 6192 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It presents example filter semantics and says operators must adapt them to their own environment.

sections.title: The Router's Two Planes
sections.content:
The control plane handles packets sent to the router and builds or sends packets originated by it. It supports routing and management functions. The forwarding plane receives packets, selects a next hop and sends them out through the appropriate interface.

Forwarding commonly uses high-performance hardware, while control-plane processing is generally performed in software on general-purpose processors. The control plane is therefore more susceptible to denial-of-service overload. The method in this RFC filters traffic destined to the router; it does not filter all traffic passing through it.
sections.plainLanguage: The forwarding plane moves packets through a router. The control plane handles routing and management, so it needs protection from too many packets addressed to the router itself.

sections.title: List the Traffic the Router Needs
sections.content:
The first step is to identify legitimate traffic destined for the control plane. The RFC's example includes routing protocols, ICMP and ICMPv6, DNS, NTP, SSH, SNMP and RADIUS replies. The list and permitted sources depend on the router's configuration and network role.

In the example, fragments are dropped, selected protocols are permitted from known sources, ICMP is rate-limited, and other traffic is rate-limited or dropped. These addresses and rates illustrate a policy; they are not requirements for every deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Start by listing the messages the router needs, such as routing updates and management traffic. The exact list depends on the router and its network.

sections.title: Apply Filters in the Forwarding Plane
sections.content:
The filter is installed in the forwarding plane so unwanted packets are stopped before using the connection to the control plane. It classifies traffic by attributes such as source address, protocol or port, then permits, rate-limits or drops each class. Counters on the classes help operators investigate attacks and troubleshoot policy.

The RFC suggests first allowing traffic and observing what reaches the control plane, then adding explicit rules for the legitimate flows found. After that audit, a default class can be configured to drop traffic that does not match an allowed class. Policies should be reviewed as network traffic changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Filters in the forwarding plane can stop or limit packets before the control plane must handle them. Operators can first observe traffic, then make the allowed list more specific.

sections.title: Trade-Offs and Special Traffic
sections.content:
A restrictive filter can also block useful traffic. Blocking all ICMP can interfere with ping and traceroute, while dropping all fragments or packets with IP options may affect a deployment that relies on them. IPv6 uses ICMPv6 for functions such as Neighbor Discovery, so its handling needs particular care.

The RFC's example rate-limits ICMP and unclassified IP traffic to 500 kbps and non-IP traffic to 250 kbps. It emphasizes that packet rate, not only bandwidth, matters for control-plane load. Operators should measure and choose limits for their own environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Filters that are too strict can block diagnostic tools or protocols the network needs. Operators must measure their traffic and choose limits that protect the router without disrupting its operation.

sections.title: Limits of Control-Plane Filtering
sections.content:
The method does not prevent spoofed packets whose source addresses match an allowed traffic class. The RFC points to edge source-address validation, ingress filtering and the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism as other protections. Protocols that reach the router still need their own cryptographic security where appropriate.

Rate-limiting ICMP can drop legitimate messages during a flood. Router-generated ICMP responses and packets that reach the control plane because their TTL or hop limit expired also need protection. These considerations are part of an overall traffic-management plan, not a replacement for edge filtering.
sections.plainLanguage: A filter does not prove that an allowed packet came from a genuine sender. The network also needs protection against spoofing, and protocols need their own authentication where appropriate.

viz.caption: The filter stops packets before they reach the control plane

layers.label: Forwarding-plane filter
layers.detail: Permits, rate-limits or drops traffic destined for the router
